title: How Feedback Keeps a System Steady

voice.text: Traffic, temperature, and water levels all change. Left alone, a small disturbance can move a system farther from the state we want.
Imagine a room on a cold day. You want it to stay at twenty degrees. That number is the target. The room itself will keep losing heat.
A thermostat measures the room, compares it with the target, and switches on the heater. Then it measures again to see what changed.
Think of the heater as the part that acts. It changes the system. The sensor closes the loop by reporting the result of that action.
When the room is too cold, the heater adds heat. As the gap shrinks, the thermostat can switch it off. That is negative feedback.
A slow sensor can report yesterday's news in miniature. If the heater keeps running while the room is already warm, the temperature can overshoot.
The same idea works on a road. A signal can measure a growing queue and give that direction more green time, then check the queue again.
Next time a system stays steady, look for three things. What is the target? What is measured? And what action reduces the gap?
